title: Hop Amplification & KV Throttling Deep Dive — Forge Labs

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-02
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (CTO, Forge Labs), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Lena Oberg (SRE)

Summary (auto): Deep-dive to triage recurring tail-latency spikes attributed to KV cache hot keys and amplified by multi-hop network paths. Focus on short-term mitigations for p99 and a pilot to validate changes.

--- Topics: p95/p99 patterns, KV cache hot shards, streaming vs non-streaming, network hop amplification, quantization latency tradeoffs ---

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick call outline — we want to walk the trace you shared, validate hypotheses about the p99 spikes, and land on a 1-week pilot. if anyone needs to add to the agenda, say now.
[00:00:12] Marta Ruiz: thanks Alex. um, yeah, high level from our side — we've got recurring p99 blips during peak synthetic workloads, roughly 3x over p95, looks like short microbursts. we sent the flamegraphs and traces last night.
[00:00:24] Priya Nair: got them, thanks. i skimmed, and an early signal is heavy retrying hitting the central KV tier — hot keys, plus some routing that turns single edge requests into multiple egress hops.
[00:00:33] Samir Patel: to add, our stack has a step function where requests pass through the edge proxy, then an internal API gateway, then to the KV tier. sometimes that path traverses a peered VPC for compliance routing — i think that's where we see an extra 20-40ms per hop.
[00:00:47] Lena Oberg: and we've observed TCP retransmits coincident with those spikes. not all the time, but often when the p99 peaks.
[00:00:56] Alex Chen: ok, that's helpful. real quick — Priya, can you confirm the model and runtime characteristics they shared? quantization, batch sizes, streaming config?
[00:01:05] Priya Nair: sure. Forge Labs is using a 16B open model, quantized to int8 for cost reasons, and they run with a mixed mode: streaming enabled for low-latency interactive flows, but non-streaming for bulk inference. batch windows tuned to 15ms by default, but they push to 50ms during throughput bursts. i noticed cold-starts on quantized kernels sometimes take an extra 30-60ms the first token, which can pollute the tail.
[00:01:31] Marta Ruiz: that cold-start was surprising. we thought quantization would be uniformly faster.
[00:01:36] Priya Nair: yeah, it's usually faster per-token, but kernel JIT path selection and cache warm-up can add latency at the start of some sequences — especially with int8 artifacts and smaller batch sizes.
[00:01:48] Samir Patel: question — does Redwood recommend streaming always? We see different behaviors.
[00:01:53] Alex Chen: short answer: it depends. streaming reduces perceived latency for the first tokens, but if you have jitter or network amplification, streaming opens a long-lived connection that can amplify head-of-line issues. also, per-request fanout to KV from streaming paths can multiply small delays.
[00:02:10] [00:02:11] Speaker 5: sorry, who is who? (laughs)
[00:02:12] Marta Ruiz: that's me.
[00:02:14] Priya Nair: back to streaming — for Forge's pattern where a single inference may require multiple KV lookups mid-generation, streaming can incur many small RPCs as tokens stream out; each of those may hit a hotspot and cause tail amplification. Non-streaming (batched) can aggregate lookups and amortize overhead.
[00:02:32] Samir Patel: hmm, in our case we do mid-token KV lookups for user-specific context. can we pipeline those with streaming?
[00:02:39] Priya Nair: you can, but then you need to ensure the KV tier can handle the small, frequent QPS pattern. otherwise it becomes hot-key magnification.
[00:02:46] Alex Chen: there's also the network path — you mentioned peered VPCs. each additional hop, especially across NATs or egress proxies, adds latency and variance. if one path experiences congestion, p99 jumps stack-wide.
[00:02:58] Lena Oberg: we mapped the topology last night. sometimes traffic goes out to the partner peering, back in via another region for compliance checks — it's a weird detour.
[00:03:07] Priya Nair: that matches some spans in the trace — a 3-hop detour where the added hop is 18-40ms and occasionally 80-120ms during background backups. that's definitely a tail amplifier.
[00:03:20] Alex Chen: okay, hypothesis A: p99 caused by KV hotspots + multi-hop amplification + occasional kernel cold-starts. Hypothesis B: batching window misconfig during bursts and streaming fanout magnifying hotspot latency. Any other hypotheses?
[00:03:34] Marta Ruiz: maybe we also have Nagle/tcp coalescing or small MTU fragmentation due to overlay network?
[00:03:40] Priya Nair: good call — MTU and path MTU black holes can cause retransmits. packet capture will confirm.
[00:03:45] Samir Patel: we use an overlay (weave) in some clusters, yes.
[00:03:48] Alex Chen: ok let's dig into mitigations. Priya, go ahead.
[00:03:52] Priya Nair: short-term mitigations: 1) local KV shard—route requests to nearest KV replica for hot keys, 2) reduce streaming fanout — allow streaming for initial tokens, then switch to non-streamed mode for heavy KV interaction, 3) reduce batching window dynamically during microbursts to avoid over-aggregation that causes backpressure, 4) ensure TCP/TLS keep-alive and max connection reuse to avoid handshake latency on short-lived streaming connections.
[00:04:17] Marta Ruiz: local KV shard — how quick to implement? we have KV in a managed cluster; can we replicate hot keys?
[00:04:24] Priya Nair: depends. if you have a tiered KV with read-replicas, we can set routing rules in the edge to favor local replicas by key hashing. Redwood's routing policy can do that without changing app code if we can map keys.
[00:04:37] Samir Patel: that would be ideal. but keys are user-scoped and we have privacy routing rules that force some keys through the compliance peered VPC.
[00:04:45] Alex Chen: right — in those cases we can do hybrid: local cache for majority non-sensitive keys, and direct-peered route for compliance keys. also consider prefix caching for repeated context snippets.
[00:04:57] [00:04:58] Speaker 6: small audio glitch here
[00:04:59] Priya Nair: medium-term: rate-limit tail QPS from streaming clients (circuit-break), implement kv request coalescing at the edge, and move high-frequency keys to memory-tier storage or an LRU local cache. For on-prem—if you prefer private deployment—we can recommend co-locating KV with the inference pool to eliminate cross-VPC hops.
[00:05:19] Marta Ruiz: co-locate sounds promising but our compliance team is hesitant. they want audit logs and KMS integration. does Redwood Private support that?
[00:05:27] Alex Chen: yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs. we can scope an on-prem pilot; but it's a heavier lift than routing tweaks.
[00:05:35] Samir Patel: about quantization cold-starts — is that something we can pre-warm?
[00:05:39] Priya Nair: yes, we can keep a small warm pool of quantized kernels or pre-touch pages on startup. there's memory and cost tradeoff but for tail control it's effective.
[00:05:48] Lena Oberg: curious — what about using smaller model shards to reduce per-token work?
[00:05:52] Priya Nair: model sharding helps throughput but can add extra network s/m between shards. for tail latency you want fewer cross-node hops. so unless shards are local, it can hurt p99.
[00:06:03] Alex Chen: let's talk about measurements — for the pilot we'll measure p50/p95/p99, and also track retransmit rate and per-hop latency. Priya, what's the recommended load pattern for the hotspot replay?
[00:06:14] Priya Nair: a 1-hour run with two phases: steady-state (60% of peak) for 30 minutes, then microburst pattern with short bursts at 120-150% peak every 30s for 30 minutes. replay should include the same key distribution to recreate hot keys.
[00:06:29] Samir Patel: ok we can provide logs and traces. we'll also turn on tcpdump for the affected nodes.
[00:06:34] [00:06:35] Marta Ruiz: small nit — our edge proxy uses HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and many short connections; would upgrading to http/2 or grpc streaming help?
[00:06:44] Priya Nair: http/2 reduces connection churn but introduces head-of-line blocking at the stream level if the underlying connection is congested. grpc over http/2 works well if you maintain connection health and have good flow control; it's not a silver bullet.
[00:06:58] Alex Chen: another practical tweak: enable connection pinning for KV requests — that way subsequent small lookups avoid creating new TCP/TLS state. Also check TLS session reuse; some of your traces showed full handshakes.
[00:07:10] Samir Patel: we do see occasional full handshakes; the edge was misconfigured to not reuse sessions for short-lived flows — will fix.
[00:07:16] [00:07:17] Lena Oberg: question on batching: if we reduce batch window during microbursts, won't throughput drop?
[00:07:22] Priya Nair: yes throughput may drop, but the goal is tail stabilization. Redwood's suggestion is an adaptive policy: during bursts reduce batch latency target and increase instance concurrency to keep overall throughput while avoiding huge tails. it's about tradeoffs.
[00:07:37] Marta Ruiz: that makes sense. for our SLOs, p99 matters more than a small throughput hit.
[00:07:41] Alex Chen: good to know. we'll prioritize tail.
[00:07:44] Priya Nair: quick note on telemetry — please enable per-request route IDs so we can correlate traces to exact KV keys and network hops. without that it's hard to map the per-token lookups.
[00:07:55] Samir Patel: we can add a header that Redwood will read — ok.
[00:07:58] [00:08:00] Alex Chen: excellent. time check: 16:08 — we've covered hypothesis and mitigations. let's capture the pilot scope and next steps.
[00:08:06] Priya Nair: Pilot proposal: 1) Provision isolated VPC route, 2) Enable local KV read-replica routing for non-compliance keys, 3) Run hotspot replay with adaptive batching and streaming fallback off by default (to compare), 4) Measure p50/p95/p99 and retransmit rates. Redwood to provide config snippets.
[00:08:25] Marta Ruiz: timeline? we can stand up the VPC route by Tuesday.
[00:08:29] Alex Chen: we'll share docs and config today; Priya will run the replay and collect logs next Thursday.
[00:08:36] Samir Patel: i'm going to reach out to the networking team for MTU and NAT timeouts.
[00:08:40] [00:08:41] Speaker 7: brief background noise
[00:08:42] Alex Chen: final housekeeping — i'll send the meeting notes, links to our streaming vs batch doc, and sample routing policy. Priya will own the replay run. Marta/Samir/Lena will provide topology and pcaps.
[00:08:56] Marta Ruiz: thanks all.
[00:08:58] Priya Nair: thanks. we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the benchmark.
[00:09:02] Alex Chen: ok closing out — see you next week.
